1. Façade: view from N-W. The cubic tuff capitals of the portal, characteristic of the architecture of the houses of the III-II century BC, support a molded epistyle with a dentilled frame. The façade is built in opus incertum of lava, the corners are of square blocks of limestone arranged horizontally and vertically. The jambs and the architrave of the shop door opened in the façade in the last period of Pompeii, have been rebuilt in concrete.   81 WAS 26620
2. Façade, detail: the entrance portal with the cast of the door. 81 WAS 26621

3. Fauces(1), floor and wall O. The passage from the fauces to the atrium (on the left in the photo) is marked by pilasters of white fluted stucco next to the rectangular threshold adorned with uadrati placed at the corner, made up of black tesserae bedded in the white beaten stone. The ornamentation of the floor of the fauces and atrium is a simple punctuation of black tesserae, a motif frequently used in passageways.  The collapse of the layer of rough plaster from the O wall made visible the preparation layer worked in relief to facilitate the adhesion of the last layer.  77 N34641

20. Tablinum (5), floor. The center of the white beaten floor dotted with large black tiles inserted in an oblique position with respect to the walls, is enriched by a black and white mosaic carpet with hourglasses: an addition from the late Republican era.  77 N34634

21. Tablinum (5), floor, section N. Even the black-and-white mosaic threshold towards the atrium (2) is an addition inserted in the late Republican period in the white beaten wall dating back to the second century BC. The series of four-pointed stars is a typical motif of the II style period. The black and white mosaic frame of the field dotted with black tiles is visible.  77 N34633

22. Tablinum (5), floor, central section. The geometric design of the mosaic carpet inserted in the late Republican era consists of two chessboards of different shapes superimposed in order to form a network of hourglasses, a motif clearly inspired by precious sectilia coverings cut with a modular system.  80 N55268

23. Cubicle (8): view from the W. The cubicle is divided into an antechamber and alcove by the floor only, with black and white geometric mosaic in the one and cocciopesto in the part intended for the bed. The wall decoration has a pergola overlooking a garden with a blue background, in which paintings or rather reproductions of reliefs (stylopinàkia) in a Dionysian or Dionysian and pharaonic statues are arranged symmetrically, visible in the middle area.  In addition, there are painted Egyptian pictures fixed above the epistyle of the pergola. It is not known whether the bronze brazier visible on the left and the kitchen pottery were found here or elsewhere in the house.  77 N34999

24. Cubicle (8), antechamber, floor. The black and white mosaic is divided into a square carpet and a rectangular threshold. The carpet depicts a six-petaled rosette included in a six-pointed star, inscribed in a double hexagon and a circle, inscribed in turn in a double square within a frame of overlapping triangles with, in the corners, squares placed per corner containing a square with concave sides. The threshold depicts six pelts leaning against each other.  (A surface area of 100 cm? includes 130 tiles). 77 N34964 15

25. Cubicle (8), N wall, middle area. There is a viburnum plant to the right of the relief with musicians in the center of the wall, and another viburnum plant behind the seated pharaonic statue which, with the one visible behind a palm tree in the right section of the wall, forms a symmetrical pair intended to lead the gaze towards the central relief.  DAIR 64.2269
26. Cubicle (8), N wall, W section, middle area, detail: the seated pharaonic statue, white with a golden-yellow uraeus on the forehead.  DAIR 64.2269

27. Cubicle (8), N wall, central section, middle area, detail: relief depicting a figure standing to the right playing a tambourine, and a harpist seated on the left with his right foot on a suppedaneum.  80 Diap. GFN5511

28. Cubicle (8), N wall, central section, upper area.  The painting depicts A pis, the sacred bull of Memphis, advancing to the W (towards the entrance door to the room). The magpie perched on the frame indicates that the bull is intended as the soul (ba) of Osiris. In Memphis, the funeral of A pis took place according to the rites of the cult of Osiris: the intestines were kept in four canopic vases, which we see above the epistyle of the pergola: two exhibited next to the painting, the other two next to the painting on the wall S. 80 GFN EK6135 18

29. Cubicle (8), N wall, central section, upper area, detail: painting with dead APIS, as indicated by the amulet of the heart that the bull wears around its neck. In Roman times it appears with the sun disk between its horns, replacing the crescent moon that was its distinctive feature in Pharaonic times.  The yellow ribbon that goes around its trunk is not reflected in Egyptian iconography. Apis' funeral was accompanied by rites, not unlike the Bacchic ones (Plut., Mor., 364E-F).  80 GFN EK6140

30. Cubicle (8), S-E corner. The black hoof, which was hidden by the bed, is painted with tufts of acanthus and fern. In the lateral intercolumns of the middle area of the wall E there are standing statues with the symbol of life (ank/) in the lowered left. Behind the left statue there is a lemon, behind the one on the right a cherry tree.  Higher up, in the axis of the columns, there are two Egyptian paintings on a white background, depicting scenes of offerings.  In the photograph taken shortly after the excavation you can see the difference between the upper pontata in intense colors and the lower one including the central picture and the side statues, in faded colors.  52 AFS A8168
31. Cubicle (8), wall E, central section, middle area. The stylopinàkion rises from an ivy omphalos, among laurel shrubs with a bird perched.   DAIR 64.2263

150. Cubicle (12), wall E, central section, middle area. The white marble monopodium highlighted by the hemicycle in the center of the reed, rests on three small disks in the green branches and is composed of a shaft with very stylized overlapping tufts, surmounted by a basin with a baccellate rim. In the basin is placed the crown of rose leaves, a symbol of the triumph of Osiris over his brother Seth, that is, of life over death.  The hydrìa placed on this crown is gold, with red and green semi-precious stones set.  The jug is depicted in such a way as to coordinate two points of view: the belly and neck are seen in profile, the long beak in prospect from above. The handle in the shape of a crowned uraeus explains the cultic use of the vessel. Apuleius (Met., 11.275.11) defines such a hydrìa in the following terms: urnula... orificium...  în canalem porrectum lungo rivulo prominebat... ansa, quam contorto nodule supersedebat aspis squameae cervicas striated tumor sublimis.  52 AFS A8142

56. Wing (4), N wall, central section, middle area: detail of the painting with Priam between Helen and Cassandra (60.5 x 67 cm). R. Bianchi Bandinelli (Bianchi Bandinelli 1950, pp. 79-80) recognizes in the depiction a Roman reworking of a Hellenistic motif, probably taken from the illustration of a manuscript, in turn echoing some well-known pictorial composition.  In this case, the Pompeian painter has succeeded in translating the scene into his own language without creating disharmony between the composition, which still draws breath from the original rhythm, and the anecdotal observation of the individual figures. These, taken each for themselves, are devoid of a coherent setting, so that they fail to be noble and epic: the epic becomes melodrama, precisely because of the contingent and prose language of the Roman painter.  But the composition remains firm due to the "maintained correspondence" of the two similar groups of warrior and woman to the left (Ajax or Ulysses and Cassandra) and to the right (Menelaus and Helen) of Priam, which constitutes the center of the painting and the perspective point for the "cone of figures" that proceeds diagonally from left to right. It should be noted that the Palladium to which Cassan-dra clings is kept in shadow and is devoid of detail, so as not to unbalance the whole composition.  The background "almost like wings of frames bent like a screen" does not create any spatial illusion. The two groups on the left and right have so far appeared in two distinct paintings of Pompeian painting: Ajax and Cassandra in a fresco that has been largely destroyed and is known only for the very brief notice given by Schulz (Schulz 1838, pp. 181 s.); Menelaus and Helen in a fragmentary and small picture (0.62 x 0.62 cm) on the E wall of the triclinium (17) of the House of PubliusCornelius Teges (I 7, 11; NS 1977, p. 48, de 22; PPP I, p. 67). The latter is a crude vulgarization, iconographically very similar, of the same group, present in the painting of the House of Menander. Completely new, however, in the House of Menander, is the grouping of the two episodes of the night of Troy. IV style.  AFS C1591

62. Wing (4), E wall, central section. Middle area: detail of the painting with Cassandra and the wooden horse (62.5 x 62.5 cm). The painting is part of the same cycle as the previous one, it is very similar to this one in terms of stylistic and structural elements and is certainly painted by the same craftsman, as is the case of the Laocoön depicted on the S wall of the same room. It represents another episode of the end of Troy: the center of the composition consists of Cassandra, dragged by the hand away from the horse by a young Phrygian; The wooden horse is in the shade on the right. Behind Cassandra is also depicted the cone of figures proceeding diagonally from left to right.  The walls, torn down to let the horse in, close the scene like a screen; in the background, with a bird's eye view, a temple with a front staircase is depicted, enclosed by a large portico. Roman taste is also recognizable here in the anecdotal traits and attributes of the individual figurines, such as the tibicine to the right of the horse or the young man with the infula and, above all, in the children who drag the horse by the ropes, in the group depicted behind Cassandra.  The representation closely resembles Virgil's story (Aen., II, 246 ff.), as does the small picture described above. Two paintings with the same subject but with a completely different iconography and drawing and pictorial trait from Pompeii should be mentioned, one of which is preserved in the National Museum of Naples, inv. Beyen [Beyen, NederlandsKunsthistorisch Jaarboek, 5, 1954] believes that the pictorial decoration of the oecus (11) belongs to a phase of transition between the III and IV styles and tends to attribute it more to the Neronian age than to the Flavian age. Various elements still lead back to the III style such as the structure of the plinth, the middle partition into fields divided by narrow bands, some with profile portraits in oval medallions of the full III style.  In the small side paintings Beyen recognizes the impressionism of the late III style. The ornamental friezes above and below the frieze with Centaurs and Lapitesses are found in the late III style but are also widely attested in the IV. The green-colored walls are typical of this transition phase.
